title: 10 Tech Protection Strategies for Your Kids and Their Friends
author: Kristy Etheridge
summary: Kristy Etheridge, features editor at Christianity Today, writes from the parent's seat about keeping children safe from unfettered internet access as a new school year begins. She opens with her ten-year-old's bedtime confession about a disturbing AI-generated video shown to him on another child's phone at baseball camp, and describes how she has become an unwilling advocate raising screen-time questions with coaches, teachers and administrators. Acknowledging the Meta settlement celebrated by Jonathan Haidt, she argues the problem is far from solved and that parents are suffering tech-talk burnout just when persistence matters most. Her central move is to frame tech advocacy as a Christian obligation to love not only one's own children but "our youngest neighbors," including the disadvantaged children most harmed by unrestricted tech. Drawing on Brad East's big-tent approach, she lists ten concrete steps: organising offline experiences with other families, pursuing beauty and truth together, asking schools, camps and activities about device policies, volunteering to supervise recess, supporting the four norms and Wait Until 8th, and asking churches to address kids and tech. (Close call between Family and Technology; Family chosen because the piece is operationally a parenting guide addressed to mothers and fathers about their own children and their children's friends.)
points: Etheridge treats tech advocacy for children as missional, extending a parent's protective duty to neighbors' kids and to families with fewer resources or children with learning disabilities.
She warns parents never to assume common-sense screen policies exist at camps, sports programs or schools, and to ask before signing children up.
Several strategies are collective rather than individual: organising offline play with other families, parent-supervised recess, and a mystery reader program to replace digital read-alouds.
She endorses the four norms (no smartphones before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools, more real-world independence) and Wait Until 8th as shared parent commitments.
She asks churches to take up kids and tech through youth discussions, parent seminars briefed by older students, or sermon series.
quotes: This has become a hobby I never wanted: initiating awkward conversations with teachers, coaches, parents, administrators, and youth leaders about kids and internet-enabled devices. I’ve learned to take nothing for granted and never to assume common-sense screen-time practices are in place, because too often they’re not.

In the absence of such rules, those of us who are less permissive with tech are left to attempt to explain violent or sexually explicit concepts to our children, rehearse together what to do if they see something troubling, and ask God to protect them when we aren’t there to shield them from evil. It’s exhausting.
I’m thrilled about the landmark settlement. But the cat is still on the loose, and parents are tired of chasing it.
Tech advocacy on behalf of kids is missional for those who follow Christ, a matter of loving not just our own families but our youngest neighbors.

Pursue beauty and truth as a family. Nothing reveals the emptiness of scrolling like real-life adventure. Walk the nature trail. Create some art. Read a good book out loud (including to older kids who may not admit it but still crave story time).

Check in with your child’s teacher, who is probably overwhelmed and at risk of burning out. Can you get some parents together to volunteer to supervise outdoor lunchtime or recess? We did this at my kids’ school when we found out students were sometimes on screens instead of socializing during downtime.

Before you sign your child up for an afterschool activity or camp, ask what kind of screen-time policies are in place (if any). Same thing for summer camps, as I’ve learned. Advocate for a no-phones policy that encompasses lunchtime and breaks.
All these recommendations are preconditioned on prayers for wisdom and humility. None of us have this all figured out. We need each other, and we need supernatural help.
